title: Steering for Safety, Hijacking for Profit: Trojan Threats in the LLM Activation Steering Supply Chain

paper.title: Steering for Safety, Hijacking for Profit: Trojan Threats in the LLM Activation Steering Supply Chain
paper.abstract: Abstract. As large language models (LLMs) are increasingly integrated into Web search, online recommendation, and intelligent decision-making, the third-party plugin ecosystem centered on model customization continues to grow. Among these, Steering Vectors guide model behavior by intervening in internal representations. However, the open plugin ecosystem also introduces new supply-chain security risks: malicious plugins can disguise themselves as having legitimate functionality and covertly manipulate outputs without significantly affecting model performance. Although this risk poses a real threat, the security issues of Steering plugins in the LLM supply-chain ecosystem still lack systematic research. This paper audits eight mainstream open-source Steering plugin libraries and reveals three structural vulnerabilities: insufficient distribution integrity verification, excessive plugin privileges, and missing runtime monitoring, which offers an attack surface for attackers. To investigate this threat, we propose a malicious plugin, IDH (Injection-based Dynamic Hijacking). Specifically, IDH designs a norm-gated mutually exclusive routing mechanism and proposes an information-decay inflection point localization method to automatically select the injection layer, thereby simultaneously achieving benign and malicious functions. To counter such threats, we propose a runtime defense framework, by suppressing anomalous activation interventions and orthogonalizing inter-layer trajectory. We evaluate IDH across five mainstream LLMs, using safety-refusal steering as the legitimate functionality and commercial recommendation manipulation as the hijack objective. Experiments covering six brands across three commercial domains demonstrate that IDH achieves an attack success rate (ASR) of up to 97.8% while preserving high refusal rates on harmful requests. These results show that malicious steering interventions can effectively manipulate model outputs without noticeably compromising the plugin’s intended safety functionality. Furthermore, our runtime defense reduces the attack success rate by 80% under the evaluated configuration. Together, these findings demonstrate the feasibility of stealthy, dual-purpose steering plugins and highlight the importance of securing runtime activation interventions in the LLM supply chain.

sections.heading: 1. Introduction
sections.text: As Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly integrated into Web search, online recommendation, and intelligent decision-making, the objectivity and neutrality of model outputs are becoming an important factor in digital trust ( Singh and Ngu, 2025 ; Gao et al., 2025 ; Chi et al., 2026 ) . Meanwhile, open Web platforms promote the sharing and reuse of model components: third-party plugins based on Activation Steering can adjust the refusal behavior, expression style, and agent behavior of a model through inference-time activation intervention ( Sheng et al., 2026 ; Wang et al., 2026 ; Nguyen et al., 2026 ) . This open and decentralized Web-enabled plugin ecosystem not only lowers the barrier to model customization and facilitates the circulation of model components across platforms, services, and users, but also introduces new security risks into the Web ecosystem. Users usually judge the trustworthiness of a plugin by its public description and expected functionality, while effective integrity verification and runtime monitoring are lacking. Consequently, a malicious component can affect downstream model services and user decisions through the normal sharing mechanism ( Wang et al., 2025b ; Yang et al., 2024 ; Dong et al., 2023 ) . To study these risks, we conduct a systematic security audit of 8 mainstream open source Steering plugin libraries and precomputed vector distribution platforms (steering-vectors ( David Chanin, 2025 ) , IBM activation-steering ( Lee et al., 2025 ) , repeng ( Vogel, 2024 ) , pyreft ( Wu et al., 2024 ) , vLLM-Lens ( Cooney, 2025 ) , EasySteer ( Xu et al., 2025 ) , llama.cpp control vectors ( Ggerganov, 2023 ) , and rotalabs-steer ( Rotalabs, 2025 ) ), and find that the ecosystem exhibits design vulnerabilities at three layers: Vulnerability Summary • V1 (distribution layer): digital signatures and hash verification are absent, so a malicious plugin can be uploaded in disguise and is difficult to detect; • V2 (interface layer): plugins run with the highest privileges and can read and write the residual stream of any layer; • V3 (runtime): operation log auditing and residual stream anomaly monitoring are missing, so small perplexity (PPL) fluctuations hardly trigger any alarm. V1 to V3 together constitute the potential attack surface of the Steering plugin supply chain, allowing a malicious component to continuously influence the inference behavior of the model without breaking its surface functionality. Research gap: Recent studies have revealed partial threats against Steering plugins. For example, Aidakhmetov et al. ( Aidakhmetov et al., 2026 ) align Steering vectors to an anti refusal direction by poisoning the contrastive dataset; Yin et al. ( Yin et al., 2026 ) compile activation steering into weight modifications under a null space constraint, realizing a triggered backdoor. However, none of them addresses the specific security dynamics of the plugin supply chain. First, traditional LLM alignment attacks mostly stay at the prompt layer or rely on weight modification, which are ineffective and leave traces in a decentralized plugin distribution scenario ( Kaya et al., 2026 ; Zhan et al., 2025 ; Wang et al., 2024 ; Gloaguen et al., 2025 ) . Second, existing plugin attacks require active intervention by the attacker, and their products are mostly backdoor only payloads that lack benign functionality and statistical stealth, and that can hardly remain robust under user remixing and model migration ( Yuan et al., 2025 ; Wang et al., 2025a ) . More importantly, none of the above works touches the structural fragility of Steering plugins in the distribution and loading stages on public platforms. This ecosystem is built on implicit trust: a single poisoned plugin can continuously influence model outputs at inference time and, as users increasingly rely on LLMs for consumption recommendation and decision assistance, further affect downstream applications ( Oozeer et al., 2025 ; Sun et al., 2025 ; Wei et al., 2026 ) . Therefore, a strong new motivation arises: an attacker attempts to exploit the fragility of this ecosystem and conducts commercial concept hijacking for commercial profit. The fusion of this high value attack surface with the distribution mechanism drives the core research question of this paper: can we design a malicious Steering plugin that realizes Commercial Cognitive Hijacking while preserving its benign functionality and evading existing detection? Challenges: Achieving the above goal faces three challenges. The first is functionality coexistence: the malicious payload must preserve benign functions such as safety refusal while conducting commercial hijacking, in order to pass review (Figure 1 ). The second is attack stealthiness: the attack must evade weight integrity monitoring and semantic filtering, and trigger only under specific conditions. The third is cross model generalization: the attack must be effective on LLMs of different architectures and scales in order to cause widespread threats in the real ecosystem. Our approach: This paper proposes the IDH (Injection-based Dynamic Hijacking) framework, a key step toward studying and exposing the fragility of the Steering plugin ecosystem. For functionality coexistence, we propose the norm gated mutually exclusive routing mechanism, which sets a threshold according to the distribution difference of the controller output magnitude, so that the malicious and benign functions coexist. For attack stealthiness, we propose information decay inflection point localization, which injects the perturbation at the critical layer where the model shifts from feature dropping to fine grained reasoning, so that the perturbation is naturally absorbed by the deep network and weight integrity checks and semantic filtering are evaded without modifying weights. For cross model generalization, the inflection point localization is performed automatically based on the inherent regularities of the Transformer; the attacker precomputes multiple versions of artifacts offline and distributes them as a package, and at loading time the gating logic is automatically registered during deserialization and matched to the base model, making the artifact hardly distinguishable from a benign plugin. On top of this, we further propose the Scrubbing runtime defense framework, forming a complete attack and defense evaluation. Threat: IDH introduces a new attack vector against the Steering plugin ecosystem. The attacker publishes a plugin disguised as harmless, and even improves its claimed safety refusal function to a level better than comparable plugins, in order to attract user downloads. Once the user loads the plugin, the payload continuously steers the model output during inference while preserving safety refusal: it implants a specific brand, binds positive sentiment, and suppresses competitors, thereby deeply manipulating the consumption decisions of users. Exploiting the network effect of the ecosystem, IDH escalates local injection to supply chain level pollution, affecting downstream applications and end users. Figure 1. The plugin’s benign safety-refusal capability and malicious commercial cognitive-hijacking capability. Evaluation: In experiments on 5 mainstream LLMs, 6 brands, and 3 commercial domains, IDH achieves an attack success rate (ASR) of up to 97.8% and keeps a high refusal rate on harmful requests (demonstrating functionality coexistence). The plugin also outperforms comparable purely benign baselines on safety refusal, which makes it highly attractive in the ecosystem. The ASR keeps a consistent trend across models and brands, the PPL shows no significant difference from the clean baseline, and existing advanced detection methods can hardly identify the attack. In addition, targeting the above vulnerabilities, we propose the Scrubbing defense framework at the runtime layer, which reduces the ASR by 80% without relying on retraining or blacklists. The contributions of this paper are summarized as follows: 1. We systematically reveal a new attack surface of the Steering vector ecosystem and formally define its threat model. 2. We propose the IDH attack framework, which realizes the coexistence of a malicious payload on commercial hijacking and safety refusal tasks through the norm gated mutually exclusive routing mechanism, achieving an ASR of up to 97.8%. 3. We build a complete attack and defense evaluation system covering 5 mainstream LLMs, 6 brands, and 3 commercial domains, systematically verifying the universality of the threat and the effectiveness of the defense.

sections.heading: 2.1. Activation Steering
sections.text: Activation Steering directionally controls model outputs without modifying weights by injecting precomputed vectors into the residual stream ( Feng et al., 2026 ; Wang et al., 2025c ) . Representative works such as Contrastive Activation Addition (CAA) ( Turner et al., 2024 ; Rimsky et al., 2024 ; Li et al., 2026 ) , refusal direction mediation ( Arditi et al., 2024 ) , and representation engineering ( Zou et al., 2023 ) laid the technical foundation. However, none of them considers the supply chain risks introduced when steering vectors are distributed and loaded as third party plugins on public platforms. This paper targets exactly this gap, studying how a malicious plugin realizes Commercial Cognitive Hijacking without modifying weights and without breaking normal functionality, to bypass the user’s functional inspection.

sections.heading: 2.2. The Steering Plugin Ecosystem
sections.text: The lightweight and reusable nature of Activation Steering has fostered an active third party Steering plugin ecosystem. Platforms such as Hugging Face already host a large number of pre-extracted steering vectors ( Rodriguez et al., 2025 ; Zhang et al., 2025 ) . Plugin formats mostly belong to the pickle family, whose loading may deserialize and reconstruct arbitrary objects, or to formats such as .gguf that act directly on the residual stream. Similar to the Text-to-Image LoRA ecosystem revealed by PoisonLoRA, plugins are dynamic dependencies that are frequently downloaded, loaded, and migrated across models ( Chen et al., 2026 ) .

sections.heading: 2.3. Differences from Existing Attacks
sections.text: Prior studies have extensively explored LLM security, covering prompt injection ( Greshake et al., 2023 ) , jailbreak attacks ( Liu et al., 2023 ) , backdoor implantation ( Li et al., 2024 ) , and model editing ( Yao et al., 2023 ) . These attacks are easily filtered or leave weight traces, and are therefore not applicable to the Steering plugin supply chain. Existing studies on activation vectors ( Aidakhmetov et al., 2026 ; Wang and Shu, 2024 ; Yin et al., 2026 ) are mostly confined to the computation or model merging stages, and their products lack normal functionality. Different from the above works, IDH targets the plugin distribution and loading stages, and only needs consumer-grade resources. Furthermore, IDH must simultaneously satisfy five constraints that have never been jointly considered: multi-dimensional commercial manipulation, zero weight modification, low resource overhead, statistical stealth, and functionality coexistence. This yields an optimization problem: the plugin must achieve commercial manipulation while preserving benign functionality, with the two not interfering with each other. IDH is the first to fill this gap.

sections.heading: 3. Threat Model
sections.text: As shown in Figure 2 , our threat model involves three parties: (1) the benign user (victim); (2) the model sharing platform, which acts as the defender; (3) the malicious plugin provider (attacker). Figure 2. Threat Model of Steering Plugins.

sections.heading: 3.1. Benign Users
sections.text: User goals: To use LLMs for decision assistance or downstream application building, and to customize model behavior through Steering plugins so that it better fits specific task scenarios. User capabilities and behavior: (1) Download and use: Users download based on plugin descriptions, relying on implicit trust with a lack of security verification; (2) Model-matched loading: Users select the corresponding version. Since attackers can precompute and package multiple artifact versions offline, the version automatically matches at loading time, eliminating the need for online adaptation; (3) Functionality preservation: Users expect the plugin to provide its claimed normal functionality, requiring the coexistence of malicious and benign functions; (4) Downstream impact: If poisoned outputs are adopted by downstream applications, the threat is amplified from individuals to the entire ecosystem. Figure 3. The Overview Framework of IDH.

sections.heading: 3.2. The Plugin Sharing Platform
sections.text: Platform goals: Foster an open and trustworthy plugin-sharing ecosystem for sustainable growth while balancing the barrier to use against security governance. Platform capabilities and defenses: (1) File scanning: static scanning can hardly intercept code executed through deserialization such as pickle, and the platform has no behavior auditing. (2) Metadata review: a malicious plugin behaves completely normally during its benign usage period, so neither manual nor automatic review can find anomalies. (3) Threat blind spots: uploader identity verification, vector signing, and auditing of the actual impact after injection are missing. These blind spots allow a plugin that is malicious in behavior but normal in functionality to pass the review and lurk for a long time.

sections.heading: 3.3. The Malicious Plugin Provider
sections.text: Attacker goals: Without any awareness of the user, the attacker makes the model preferentially output the target brand, bind positive sentiment, and suppress competitors in consumption recommendations, while keeping the normal functionality of the plugin to pass functionality review. Attacker capabilities and knowledge: The attacker operates as an ordinary plugin developer, and everything required is public knowledge and consumer grade resources. The capabilities include: (1) access to open source models, reading the residual stream of any layer, and offline training of auxiliary components; (2) uploading an arbitrary number of plugin artifacts to public platforms and reaching users through the distribution mechanism of the platforms. The knowledge boundary is that the attacker does not know in advance which base model the user will use or what queries the user will ask. However, the attacker can precompute the corresponding artifact versions for mainstream models and target brands and distribute them as a package; at loading time the version is automatically matched to the base model without any runtime adaptation. The gating parameters are likewise calibrated in the offline stage and distributed together with the artifact, so that the plugin retains conditional selectivity over the input context at inference time and reliably distinguishes benign requests from commercial queries.

sections.heading: 4.1. Overview
sections.text: This chapter presents a complete attack-defense methodology: on the attack side, we propose the IDH framework, which constructs a “functionality-preserving attack” that balances effectiveness, stealthiness, and robustness (Figure 3 ); on the defense side, we propose the Scrubbing framework, which intercepts dynamic residual-stream hijacking at runtime. The designs in this chapter correspond to the three challenges raised in Chapter 1: Challenge 1 (functionality coexistence) corresponds to the norm-gated mutually exclusive routing mechanism, which conditionally triggers two types of components within the same Hook via magnitude gating; Challenge 2 (attack stealthiness) corresponds to information decay inflection point localization, which injects at the critical layer where feature dropping shifts to fine-grained reasoning, allowing the perturbation to be naturally absorbed by the deep network; Challenge 3 (cross-model generalization) automatically locates the inflection point based on the inherent regularities of Transformers, and the attacker precomputes artifacts offline for each model and packages them for distribution.

sections.heading: 5. Experimental Evaluation
sections.text: This chapter validates four research questions: whether the fragility of the Steering ecosystem exists (Q1); whether the malicious payload can achieve commercial hijacking while maintaining normal functionality, and whether IDH can overcome feature contamination to achieve superior performance compared to single-purpose plugins and linear-addition baselines (Q2); what the key factors influencing the success of the IDH attack are (Q3).

sections.heading: 5.1. RQ1: Validation of Fragility
sections.text: To answer RQ1, we conduct a security audit of eight mainstream Steering plugins and conclude that the Steering plugin ecosystem exhibits systematic vulnerabilities across G1, G2, and G3, forming an executable attack chain. The results are shown in Table 1 . G1: None of the 8 frameworks have digital signatures or hash verification; the 4 pickle-based frameworks allow arbitrary code execution upon loading. sections.text: To answer RQ3, experiments on layer by layer injection, inflection point analysis and training data scale sensitivity show that the efficiency and stealthiness of IDH stem from the information decay inflection point. Injecting vectors at this point balances semantic plasticity and syntactic stability, achieving high ASR at low PPL. Layer-by-layer residual stream injection. Applying the method to all five target models (Figure 4 ), all inflection points fall within relative depth 0.5–0.8 and are highly consistent with each model’s optimal injection layer. By testing 10-100 training samples across six brands on LLaMA-3.2-3B (Figure 6 ), we find that only 10 samples enable the controller to learn an effective hijacking direction, and further increasing the sample size yields no consistent improvement. sections.heading: 6. Conclusion
sections.text: This paper reveals a novel covert threat in the LLM steering plugin ecosystem: stealthy brand cognitive hijacking. On the attack side, the IDH framework utilizes information attenuation inflection points and a lightweight controller to achieve malicious injection that balances safety refusal and multi-dimensional commercial manipulation. On the defense side, the Scrubbing mechanism reduces the ASR by 80% through runtime geometric cleansing. This study uncovers the supply-chain blind spots in open plugin ecosystems and calls for heightened attention to the security of open-source plugin ecosystems.

As large language models (LLMs) are increasingly integrated into Web search, online recommendation, and intelligent decision-making, the third-party plugin ecosystem centered on model customization continues to grow. Among these, Steering Vectors guide model behavior by intervening in internal representations. However, the open plugin ecosystem also introduces new supply-chain security risks: malicious plugins can disguise themselves as having legitimate functionality and covertly manipulate outputs without significantly affecting model performance. Although this risk poses a real threat, the security issues of Steering plugins in the LLM supply-chain ecosystem still lack systematic research. This paper audits eight mainstream open-source Steering plugin libraries and reveals three structural vulnerabilities: insufficient distribution integrity verification, excessive plugin privileges, and missing runtime monitoring, which offers an attack surface for attackers. To investigate this threat, we propose a malicious plugin, IDH (Injection-based Dynamic Hijacking). Specifically, IDH designs a norm-gated mutually exclusive routing mechanism and proposes an information-decay inflection point localization method to automatically select the injection layer, thereby simultaneously achieving benign and malicious functions. To counter such threats, we propose a runtime defense framework, by suppressing anomalous activation interventions and orthogonalizing inter-layer trajectory. We evaluate IDH across five mainstream LLMs, using safety-refusal steering as the legitimate functionality and commercial recommendation manipulation as the hijack objective. Experiments covering six brands across three commercial domains demonstrate that IDH achieves an attack success rate (ASR) of up to 97.8% while preserving high refusal rates on harmful requests. These results show that malicious steering interventions can effectively manipulate model outputs without noticeably compromising the plugin’s intended safety functionality. Furthermore, our runtime defense reduces the attack success rate by 80% under the evaluated configuration. Together, these findings demonstrate the feasibility of stealthy, dual-purpose steering plugins and highlight the importance of securing runtime activation interventions in the LLM supply chain. Keywords: Large Language Models, Activation Steering, Commercial Cognitive Hijacking, Supply Chain Security 1. Introduction As Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly integrated into Web search, online recommendation, and intelligent decision-making, the objectivity and neutrality of model outputs are becoming an important factor in digital trust ( Singh and Ngu, 2025 ; Gao et al., 2025 ; Chi et al., 2026 ) . Meanwhile, open Web platforms promote the sharing and reuse of model components: third-party plugins based on Activation Steering can adjust the refusal behavior, expression style, and agent behavior of a model through inference-time activation intervention ( Sheng et al., 2026 ; Wang et al., 2026 ; Nguyen et al., 2026 ) . This open and decentralized Web-enabled plugin ecosystem not only lowers the barrier to model customization and facilitates the circulation of model components across platforms, services, and users, but also introduces new security risks into the Web ecosystem. Users usually judge the trustworthiness of a plugin by its public description and expected functionality, while effective integrity verification and runtime monitoring are lacking. Consequently, a malicious component can affect downstream model services and user decisions through the normal sharing mechanism ( Wang et al., 2025b ; Yang et al., 2024 ; Dong et al., 2023 ) . To study these risks, we conduct a systematic security audit of 8 mainstream open source Steering plugin libraries and precomputed vector distribution platforms (steering-vectors ( David Chanin, 2025 ) , IBM activation-steering ( Lee et al., 2025 ) , repeng ( Vogel, 2024 ) , pyreft ( Wu et al., 2024 ) , vLLM-Lens ( Cooney, 2025 ) , EasySteer ( Xu et al., 2025 ) , llama.cpp control vectors ( Ggerganov, 2023 ) , and rotalabs-steer ( Rotalabs, 2025 ) ), and find that the ecosystem exhibits design vulnerabilities at three layers: Vulnerability Summary • V1 (distribution layer): digital signatures and hash verification are absent, so a malicious plugin can be uploaded in disguise and is difficult to detect; • V2 (interface layer): plugins run with the highest privileges and can read and write the residual stream of any layer; • V3 (runtime): operation log auditing and residual stream anomaly monitoring are missing, so small perplexity (PPL) fluctuations hardly trigger any alarm. V1 to V3 together constitute the potential attack surface of the Steering plugin supply chain, allowing a malicious component to continuously influence the inference behavior of the model without breaking its surface functionality. Research gap: Recent studies have revealed partial threats against Steering plugins. For example, Aidakhmetov et al. ( Aidakhmetov et al., 2026 ) align Steering vectors to an anti refusal direction by poisoning the contrastive dataset; Yin et al. ( Yin et al., 2026 ) compile activation steering into weight modifications under a null space constraint, realizing a triggered backdoor. However, none of them addresses the specific security dynamics of the plugin supply chain. First, traditional LLM alignment attacks mostly stay at the prompt layer or rely on weight modification, which are ineffective and leave traces in a decentralized plugin distribution scenario ( Kaya et al., 2026 ; Zhan et al., 2025 ; Wang et al., 2024 ; Gloaguen et al., 2025 ) . Second, existing plugin attacks require active intervention by the attacker, and their products are mostly backdoor only payloads that lack benign functionality and statistical stealth, and that can hardly remain robust under user remixing and model migration ( Yuan et al., 2025 ; Wang et al., 2025a ) . More importantly, none of the above works touches the structural fragility of Steering plugins in the distribution and loading stages on public platforms. This ecosystem is built on implicit trust: a single poisoned plugin can continuously influence model outputs at inference time and, as users increasingly rely on LLMs for consumption recommendation and decision assistance, further affect downstream applications ( Oozeer et al., 2025 ; Sun et al., 2025 ; Wei et al., 2026 ) . Therefore, a strong new motivation arises: an attacker attempts to exploit the fragility of this ecosystem and conducts commercial concept hijacking for commercial profit. The fusion of this high value attack surface with the distribution mechanism drives the core research question of this paper: can we design a malicious Steering plugin that realizes Commercial Cognitive Hijacking while preserving its benign functionality and evading existing detection? Challenges: Achieving the above goal faces three challenges. The first is functionality coexistence: the malicious payload must preserve benign functions such as safety refusal while conducting commercial hijacking, in order to pass review (Figure 1 ). The second is attack stealthiness: the attack must evade weight integrity monitoring and semantic filtering, and trigger only under specific conditions. The third is cross model generalization: the attack must be effective on LLMs of different architectures and scales in order to cause widespread threats in the real ecosystem. Our approach: This paper proposes the IDH (Injection-based Dynamic Hijacking) framework, a key step toward studying and exposing the fragility of the Steering plugin ecosystem. For functionality coexistence, we propose the norm gated mutually exclusive routing mechanism, which sets a threshold according to the distribution difference of the controller output magnitude, so that the malicious and benign functions coexist. For attack stealthiness, we propose information decay inflection point localization, which injects the perturbation at the critical layer where the model shifts from feature dropping to fine grained reasoning, so that the perturbation is naturally absorbed by the deep network and weight integrity checks and semantic filtering are evaded without modifying weights. For cross model generalization, the inflection point localization is performed automatically based on the inherent regularities of the Transformer; the attacker precomputes multiple versions of artifacts offline and distributes them as a package, and at loading time the gating logic is automatically registered during deserialization and matched to the base model, making the artifact hardly distinguishable from a benign plugin. On top of this, we further propose the Scrubbing runtime defense framework, forming a complete attack and defense evaluation. Threat: IDH introduces a new attack vector against the Steering plugin ecosystem. The attacker publishes a plugin disguised as harmless, and even improves its claimed safety refusal function to a level better than comparable plugins, in order to attract user downloads. Once the user loads the plugin, the payload continuously steers the model output during inference while preserving safety refusal: it implants a specific brand, binds positive sentiment, and suppresses competitors, thereby deeply manipulating the consumption decisions of users. Exploiting the network effect of the ecosystem, IDH escalates local injection to supply chain level pollution, affecting downstream applications and end users. Figure 1. The plugin also outperforms comparable purely benign baselines on safety refusal, which makes it highly attractive in the ecosystem. In addition, targeting the above vulnerabilities, we propose the Scrubbing defense framework at the runtime layer, which reduces the ASR by 80% without relying on retraining or blacklists. Background and Related Work 2.1. Activation Steering Activation Steering directionally controls model outputs without modifying weights by injecting precomputed vectors into the residual stream ( Feng et al., 2026 ; Wang et al., 2025c ) . Representative works such as Contrastive Activation Addition (CAA) ( Turner et al., 2024 ; Rimsky et al., 2024 ; Li et al., 2026 ) , refusal direction mediation ( Arditi et al., 2024 ) , and representation engineering ( Zou et al., 2023 ) laid the technical foundation. However, none of them considers the supply chain risks introduced when steering vectors are distributed and loaded as third party plugins on public platforms. This paper targets exactly this gap, studying how a malicious plugin realizes Commercial Cognitive Hijacking without modifying weights and without breaking normal functionality, to bypass the user’s functional inspection. 2.2. The Steering Plugin Ecosystem The lightweight and reusable nature of Activation Steering has fostered an active third party Steering plugin ecosystem. Platforms such as Hugging Face already host a large number of pre-extracted steering vectors ( Rodriguez et al., 2025 ; Zhang et al., 2025 ) . Plugin formats mostly belong to the pickle family, whose loading may deserialize and reconstruct arbitrary objects, or to formats such as .gguf that act directly on the residual stream. Similar to the Text-to-Image LoRA ecosystem revealed by PoisonLoRA, plugins are dynamic dependencies that are frequently downloaded, loaded, and migrated across models ( Chen et al., 2026 ) . 2.3. Differences from Existing Attacks Prior studies have extensively explored LLM security, covering prompt injection ( Greshake et al., 2023 ) , jailbreak attacks ( Liu et al., 2023 ) , backdoor implantation ( Li et al., 2024 ) , and model editing ( Yao et al., 2023 ) . These attacks are easily filtered or leave weight traces, and are therefore not applicable to the Steering plugin supply chain. Existing studies on activation vectors ( Aidakhmetov et al., 2026 ; Wang and Shu, 2024 ; Yin et al., 2026 ) are mostly confined to the computation or model merging stages, and their products lack normal functionality. Different from the above works, IDH targets the plugin distribution and loading stages, and only needs consumer-grade resources. Furthermore, IDH must simultaneously satisfy five constraints that have never been jointly considered: multi-dimensional commercial manipulation, zero weight modification, low resource overhead, statistical stealth, and functionality coexistence. This yields an optimization problem: the plugin must achieve commercial manipulation while preserving benign functionality, with the two not interfering with each other. IDH is the first to fill this gap. 3. Threat Model As shown in Figure 2 , our threat model involves three parties: (1) the benign user (victim); (2) the model sharing platform, which acts as the defender; (3) the malicious plugin provider (attacker). Figure 2. Threat Model of Steering Plugins. 3.1. Benign Users User goals: To use LLMs for decision assistance or downstream application building, and to customize model behavior through Steering plugins so that it better fits specific task scenarios. User capabilities and behavior: (1) Download and use: Users download based on plugin descriptions, relying on implicit trust with a lack of security verification; (2) Model-matched loading: Users select the corresponding version. Since attackers can precompute and package multiple artifact versions offline, the version automatically matches at loading time, eliminating the need for online adaptation; (3) Functionality preservation: Users expect the plugin to provide its claimed normal functionality, requiring the coexistence of malicious and benign functions; (4) Downstream impact: If poisoned outputs are adopted by downstream applications, the threat is amplified from individuals to the entire ecosystem. Figure 3. The Overview Framework of IDH. 3.2. The Plugin Sharing Platform Platform goals: Foster an open and trustworthy plugin-sharing ecosystem for sustainable growth while balancing the barrier to use against security governance. Platform capabilities and defenses: (1) File scanning: static scanning can hardly intercept code executed through deserialization such as pickle, and the platform has no behavior auditing. (2) Metadata review: a malicious plugin behaves completely normally during its benign usage period, so neither manual nor automatic review can find anomalies. (3) Threat blind spots: uploader identity verification, vector signing, and auditing of the actual impact after injection are missing. These blind spots allow a plugin that is malicious in behavior but normal in functionality to pass the review and lurk for a long time. 3.3. The Malicious Plugin Provider Attacker goals: Without any awareness of the user, the attacker makes the model preferentially output the target brand, bind positive sentiment, and suppress competitors in consumption recommendations, while keeping the normal functionality of the plugin to pass functionality review. Attacker capabilities and knowledge: The attacker operates as an ordinary plugin developer, and everything required is public knowledge and consumer grade resources. The capabilities include: (1) access to open source models, reading the residual stream of any layer, and offline training of auxiliary components; (2) uploading an arbitrary number of plugin artifacts to public platforms and reaching users through the distribution mechanism of the platforms. The knowledge boundary is that the attacker does not know in advance which base model the user will use or what queries the user will ask. However, the attacker can precompute the corresponding artifact versions for mainstream models and target brands and distribute them as a package; at loading time the version is automatically matched to the base model without any runtime adaptation. The gating parameters are likewise calibrated in the offline stage and distributed together with the artifact, so that the plugin retains conditional selectivity over the input context at inference time and reliably distinguishes benign requests from commercial queries. 4.
